title: How do you decide whether a client should make a big investment?
description: "Should the client make this investment?" A new plant, more capacity, a system, a store or a piece of equipment.
hook: Decide whether a client should make a big investment by checking four things: whether it really needs the investment, whether the investment pays back within its useful life, whether a cheaper alternative would do the job, and whether the client can deliver it. Put numbers on the second question with payback and, where time matters, NPV. Here is the structure, how to adapt it, and a worked example where the payback looks fine but the decision is tight.
body:
When you will use it

Use it when the client is weighing a large upfront spend: a new plant, extra capacity, a store, an IT system or a piece of equipment. It is a decide question: you test the idea against a few yes-or-no questions, put a number on it, and end with a clear answer. See which framework to use for each type of question for the other families.

Ask this first

What does it cost upfront, what does it change (revenue, costs or both), and how long will it last?

Those three facts give you the skeleton of the calculation. Ask also whether the client has a payback target or a required return.

The structure

  • Do we need it?
    • Is the demand real and lasting?
    • Can existing assets do more: fix bottlenecks, add shifts?
  • Will it pay?
    • Upfront and running costs
    • Extra revenue or savings
    • What happens to prices if rivals add capacity too
  • Is there a better alternative?
    • Outsource or subcontract
    • Lease or rent instead of buying
    • Redesign the process
  • Can we deliver it?
    • Time to build
    • Skills and execution risks

Make it your own

Three formulas cover most investment cases:

  • Payback = upfront cost ÷ yearly net gain. Quick, and easy to compare with the asset's life.
  • Break-even volume = upfront cost ÷ extra margin per unit. Useful when the gain depends on selling more.
  • NPV = today's value of the future gains minus the upfront cost. Use it when the gains are spread over several years, because a dollar in year five is worth less than a dollar today.

Payback tells you how fast you get your money back. It does not tell you whether the investment creates value. Our explainer on payback and NPV covers the difference in more depth.

A short worked example

A manufacturer can buy a $2M machine that should save $650k a year in labour and scrap. Maintenance adds $100k a year, and the machine lasts five years. The client's cost of capital is 10%. The figures are illustrative.

Payback. Net yearly gain: $650k − $100k = $550k. Payback: $2M ÷ $550k ≈ 3.6 years, inside the five-year life. It looks comfortable.

NPV. The value today of $550k a year for five years at 10% is about $550k × 3.79 ≈ $2.085M. (3.79 is the sum of 1 ÷ 1.1, 1 ÷ 1.1², and so on to year five.) NPV ≈ $2.085M − $2M = about $85k. Positive, but only just.

Break-even saving. For NPV to be zero, the net gain must be $2M ÷ 3.79 ≈ $528k a year, so gross savings must reach about $628k. The vendor promises $650k. The margin for error is about $22k a year, roughly 3% of the promised saving.

Stress-test. If savings come in 20% lower ($520k), the net gain is $420k, payback stretches to about 4.8 years, and NPV falls to about −$408k. A machine that "pays back in 3.6 years" destroys value if the vendor is moderately optimistic.

Recommendation: do not approve on the vendor's numbers alone. Ask for evidence from similar plants, negotiate a performance guarantee or a lower price, and compare with leasing or a process redesign that might deliver most of the saving for less capital.

Strong and weak answers

A weak answer stops at payback:

It pays back in 3.6 years and lasts five, so they should buy it.

A strong answer tests how much the answer depends on one assumption:

Payback is 3.6 years, but at a 10% cost of capital the NPV is only about $85k. If savings come in 20% short, it loses money, so I'd want a performance guarantee before signing.

The mistakes to avoid

  1. Approving new capacity before squeezing existing capacity. Extra shifts or fixing a bottleneck may be far cheaper.
  2. Treating payback as the whole answer. Check NPV when gains are spread over years.
  3. Forgetting running costs. Maintenance, staff and energy reduce the yearly gain.
  4. Ignoring alternatives. Leasing, outsourcing or redesign can deliver the benefit with less risk. The outsourcing tip shows how to compare.

Practise with real prompts

1. Should a car maker build its own battery plant?

Show the answer
  • Need: our battery demand and supply security; suppliers' prices and lead times.
  • Make against buy: plant cost per kWh against buying; payback and NPV.
  • Risks: fast-changing technology; running a plant at scale.
  • Alternatives: joint venture, long-term supply contracts, a stake in a supplier.

Where to start: cost per kWh, make against buy, over the life of the plant.

The trap: ignoring that battery technology may change before the plant pays back.

2. Should an airline launch a co-branded credit card?

Show the answer
  • Customer value: who would use it, how they earn and redeem points.
  • Economics: what the bank pays per card and per point, against the cost of reward seats and marketing.
  • Partner: which bank, terms, exclusivity, risk sharing.
  • Risks: brand damage if the bank treats customers badly; too many free seats.

Where to start: what the bank pays per point compared with what a reward seat costs.

The trap: treating it as a brand decision when it is mainly a points business.

3. Should a supermarket open dark stores for 15-minute delivery?

Show the answer
  • Demand: orders per dark store per day; density of orders within a 15-minute radius.
  • Economics per order: basket size and delivery fee against picking, delivery and rent per order.
  • Cannibalisation: orders taken from our own stores and online service.
  • Competition and operations: rivals' pricing; staffing and stock.

Where to start: economics per order. At low volume, the fixed rent and staff cost per order is high.

The trap: assuming every order is new rather than taken from our own stores.
